Obsidian 1.0 broke a CSS snippet that stopped the cursor from blinking in Vim mode; the user asked for it to be fixed.
As an outliner, Logseq is too opinionated. Obsidian is less strict and lets the user mix a bit of Zettelkasten, some daily notes, and old-fashioned folder structures for projects as they please.
Logseq's interconnectedness made one user lose confidence in the system. "With Obsidian I know that a note is a file. Less convenient but simple and reliable." They miss Logseq's outlining mode.
Obsidian is my favorite app. My only missing feature is better PDF support like Logseq's: embedding PDFs and annotating them with area highlights and math notation.

Used Obsidian to run tabletop RPG sessions with folders of monsters, encounters, and world notes; dropping them inline for a session note was "monumentally useful." It also replaced Sublime plus a directory for dev notes: fast and gets out of the way.

Built-in vim mode works surprisingly well, with minor cursor-blinking glitches. The plugin community and API let the user extract metadata and publish metrics to CloudWatch, something Zettlr and Bear lacked.
One user dislikes the aesthetics and won't use it because it's Electron, preferring native apps like Bear and Noteplan, which have nicer UX/UI, especially on mobile.
Daily driver for over a year. Found the graph view gimmicky for their workflow, but the rest of the features are super polished.
Moved from Google Docs to Obsidian while de-Googling. Notes are stored only on their machine and sync service, and as plain text they can outlive Obsidian itself.
Bases is not as 'kitchen sink' comprehensive as Dataview yet, but it's about a 90% replacement and a ton faster and more responsive.
Used Bases in beta for a month for D&D campaign notes; it made getting an overview of NPCs (name, pronouns, picture, race, class) much easier. The dev team was very responsive to beta feedback.

The Obsidian Android app doesn't seem to save files to storage until the note unloads, which can break git syncing if you pull mid-edit. Another user lost last lines after swiping the app away; adding trailing newlines mostly fixed it.
No decent RAG functionality, but the Text-Generator plugin, with a template pulling links and backlinks into context, has been the user's most productive LLM interface for years.
Obsidian plugins have no sandboxing; every plugin has full access to your computer. One user's company needs sandboxed apps for sensitive data, so they consider community plugins too risky.
Drawing ('Ink' plugin) is a big miss in the standard feature set, the only thing missed from OneNote, which is "horrible in every other way compared to Obsidian."
The built-in search doesn't work well for one user. The Copilot plugin works with self-hosted LLMs, but its author pushes their own paid service.
Canvas uses JSON .canvas files, its first move away from markdown; one user hopes this isn't a trend toward proprietary formats.
On Windows you can't create a desktop shortcut to open a specific vault because a vault is a folder, not a file. The standard F2 rename shortcut also doesn't work.
One user can't grasp how the small team consistently releases such high-quality software, almost for free.
Migrated from Roam to Obsidian: owns their files, gets constant updates and bug fixes, and the community is nice.
